courseEvidence.name: Personal & Professional Development
courseEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courseEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
courseEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courseEvidence.contribution: Develops academic writing, research literacy and civic reflection.

courseEvidence.name: Accounting & Corporate Finance
courseEvidence.description2: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces financial accounting, management accounting and investment appraisal, including accounting's social role and accountability implications. Students record transactions, prepare and interpret financial statements, and analyze performance and financing. The course then examines costing, pricing, budgeting, organizational control and sustainable management accounting. Investment decisions are evaluated using accounting and discounted-cash-flow measures. A case study analyzes the misuse of an accounting principle and its financial-statement effects.
courseEvidence.topics: Accounting and accountability; Financial reporting frameworks; Accrual accounting; Assets, liabilities and equity; Financial statements and cash flows; Accounting judgements and estimates; Costing and pricing; Budgeting and performance indicators; Organizational control; Sustainable management accounting; Investment appraisal; Accounting misuse
courseEvidence.methods: Double-entry bookkeeping; Year-end accounting adjustments; Financial-statement preparation; Financial-ratio analysis; Variance analysis; Accounting rate of return and payback calculations; Net present value and internal rate of return; Cost-of-capital analysis; Accounting case analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Teaches accounting theory and analysis of financial statements as a business-information complement to economic applications. Its actual profile does not establish capital budgeting, asset pricing, financial mathematics or corporate-finance theory.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Economics
courseEvidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
courseEvidence.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling
courseEvidence.contribution: introduces supply and demand, game theory, consumer and firm theory and market structure, the economic theory on which mathematical economics builds

courseEvidence.name: International Macroeconomics
courseEvidence.description2: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines short-, medium- and long-run macroeconomic dynamics and policy, including international dimensions. Students study goods, financial and labour markets, inflation and unemployment, economic growth, expectations and the open economy. IS-LM and IS-LM-PC models connect markets and policy effects. Algebraic and graphical analysis and interpretation of macroeconomic indicators support the evaluation of economic developments and fiscal and monetary policy.
courseEvidence.topics: Goods and financial markets; Labour markets; Phillips curve; IS-LM and IS-LM-PC models; Economic growth; Saving and capital accumulation; Technological progress; Expectations; Open-economy macroeconomics; Fiscal and monetary policy; Business cycles and economic crises
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical macroeconomic analysis; IS-LM and IS-LM-PC modelling; Macroeconomic data and indicator analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: analyses national income, growth, inflation, unemployment, business cycles and fiscal and monetary policy, the economy-wide dynamics to which economic models are applied

courseEvidence.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
courseEvidence.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.
courseEvidence.topics: Choice under uncertainty; Non-egoistic preferences; Cognitive limitations; Monopoly; Imperfect competition and strategic behaviour; Labour markets; Capital markets; General equilibrium; Market efficiency; Externalities; Government intervention
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic microeconomic analysis; Graphical economic analysis; Critical evaluation of economic research
courseEvidence.contribution: develops advanced microeconomic theory: decisions under uncertainty, imperfect competition and strategic behaviour, general equilibrium and market efficiency, the subject matter that mathematical economics formalises

courseEvidence.name: Public Economics
courseEvidence.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
courseEvidence.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
courseEvidence.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research
courseEvidence.contribution: analyses market failure, public goods, externalities and taxation with theoretical models and empirical evidence, applying welfare economics to the choice of optimal policy

courseEvidence.name: Econometrics
courseEvidence.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courseEvidence.contribution: teaches OLS, GLS and instrumental-variables estimation, t, F and LM tests and Monte Carlo study of sampling distributions, applying statistical estimation and testing to data and requiring an empirical paper

courseEvidence.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courseEvidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
courseEvidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
courseEvidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: introduces research design and descriptive and inferential statistics up to analysis of variance, the applied statistical inference that complements mathematical probability and estimation

courseEvidence.name: Decision-making in AI
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops the mathematical foundations of intelligent-agent decisions under uncertainty. Probability and Bayesian networks support belief updating and inference, while temporal models address changing environments. Decision theory, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems connect uncertainty to policies and expected utility. Multi-agent decisions introduce strategic and collective interaction, and probabilistic programming provides a framework for expressing models. Students work through equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.
courseEvidence.topics: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' rule; Bayesian networks; Temporal probabilistic models; Hidden Markov models and dynamic Bayesian networks; Expected utility; Markov and partially observable decision processes; Exploration-exploitation trade-offs and bandits; Competitive and cooperative multi-agent interaction; Negotiation, auctions and voting; Probabilistic programming
courseEvidence.methods: Probabilistic inference; Bayesian-network modelling; Temporal probabilistic modelling; Expected-utility analysis; Sequential decision modelling; Game-theoretic analysis; Probabilistic programming
courseEvidence.contribution: Studies AI planning with uncertainty, partial observability and resource constraints. It applies formal decision techniques, but is not a course in stochastic-process models or VU dynamical-systems theory.

courseEvidence.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
courseEvidence.description2: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
courseEvidence.topics: Propositional and predicate logic; Truth tables and logical laws; Set theory; Boolean algebra and circuits; Quantifiers; Functions and relations; Proof strategies; Mathematical induction; Recursive definitions; Games without chance and winning strategies; Process modelling
courseEvidence.methods: Truth-table analysis; Direct proof and proof by cases; Proof by contrapositive and contradiction; Proof with quantifiers; Mathematical induction; Formal process and game modelling
courseEvidence.contribution: Introduces logic, discrete structures and patterns for mathematical decision-making and algorithm construction. The documented profile does not establish the full graph-theory, combinatorics or proof-assessment sequence of VU Discrete Mathematics.

courseEvidence.name: Optimization Methods in AI
courseEvidence.description2: Covers computational methods for search problems in complex and adversarial environments. Includes uninformed and informed search, local and global search, adversarial games and constraint satisfaction problems.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies search and optimization for rational agents in known, complex and adversarial environments. Students move from uninformed and heuristic search to local and global optimization, first- and second-order methods and population approaches. Adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimization extend the toolkit. Laboratories and projects require algorithm tracing, implementation and evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.
courseEvidence.topics: Intelligent and rational agents; Uninformed and informed search; Heuristic functions; Search in complex environments; Local and global optimization; First- and second-order optimization; Population methods; Adversarial games; Constraint satisfaction; Linear programming; Discrete optimization
courseEvidence.methods: Uninformed and heuristic search; Local and global search; First- and second-order optimization; Population-based optimization; Adversarial search; Monte Carlo tree search; Constraint-satisfaction algorithms; Linear programming; Discrete optimization; Algorithm implementation and experimental evaluation
courseEvidence.contribution: Teaches discrete/continuous search and constraint satisfaction, with projects in convex optimisation and linear/nonlinear programming. These are substantive computational mathematical methods, without claiming the named hospital or delivery-route examples are taught.

courseEvidence.name: Reinforcement Learning
courseEvidence.description2: Explores reinforcement learning. Covers theoretical frameworks and algorithms and requires students to implement algorithms and build agents using neural networks that learn through trial and error.
courseEvidence.contribution: treats reinforcement-learning frameworks and algorithms and has students implement agents that learn optimal behaviour from sequential trial-and-error data

courseEvidence.name: Database Management Systems
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
courseEvidence.contribution: introduces relational database theory, SQL, normalisation and query processing, the data-management layer of data science

courseEvidence.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
courseEvidence.description2: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies algorithm design and analysis, emphasizing how algorithms and data structures affect execution time. Students examine sorting, searching, random-number generation, string matching and graph algorithms, then study computability, verification, reductions and complexity classes. Programming and mathematical exercises develop algorithmic understanding, while projects require students to design, execute and report experimental investigations of performance.
courseEvidence.topics: Abstract data structures; Asymptotic complexity; Random-number generation and sampling; Sorting and stability; String matching and finite automata; Sequential and binary search; Graph traversal; Shortest paths and spanning trees; Topological sorting; Computability and Turing machines; Polynomial-time verification; Reductions and complexity hierarchy
courseEvidence.methods: Asymptotic time-complexity analysis; Experimental algorithm benchmarking; Algorithm implementation and tracing; Random-number generator testing; Breadth-first and depth-first search; Graph algorithm analysis; Computational reductions
courseEvidence.contribution: teaches the design and performance analysis of algorithms and data structures, applying discrete mathematics and mathematical reasoning about efficiency to computational problems

courseEvidence.name: Advanced Algorithms
courseEvidence.description2: Studies modern algebraic algorithms and optimization methods. Emphasises algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling of computational problems.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies algebraic algorithms and advanced optimization methods through mathematical reasoning, implementation and experimental analysis. Fast and exact arithmetic, number-theoretic algorithms, matrix multiplication and Fourier transformation lead into hashing, greedy methods, dynamic programming and network flows. Laboratories develop algorithmic understanding, while projects investigate exact computing and optimization, including hypotheses, measured performance and sensitivity analysis.
courseEvidence.topics: Asymptotic time complexity; Fast integer arithmetic; Greatest common divisors and modular arithmetic; Chinese remainder theorem; Arbitrary-precision integers; Primality and factorization; Fast matrix multiplication; Polynomials and Fourier transformation; Hashing and Bloom filters; Greedy algorithms and coding; Dynamic programming; Flow networks; Network science
courseEvidence.methods: Asymptotic and empirical complexity analysis; Euclidean algorithm; Primality testing and factorization; Fast arithmetic and matrix algorithms; Fast Fourier transformation; Hashing; Greedy optimization; Dynamic programming; Maximum-flow algorithms; Algorithmic experimental design; Sensitivity analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: studies modern algebraic algorithms, fast and arbitrary-precision arithmetic and advanced optimisation methods, giving computational contact with algebraic structures; it complements but does not replace courses in abstract algebra

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Data Science
courseEvidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
courseEvidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
courseEvidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: develops data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation for tabular, spatial and text data in code and ends with an independent data-analysis project answering a research question

courseEvidence.name: Machine Learning
courseEvidence.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
courseEvidence.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
courseEvidence.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation
courseEvidence.contribution: Develops regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree methods, support-vector machines and clustering. This is a substantial statistical-learning contribution; it is not the full mathematical theory of statistical estimators.

courseEvidence.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
courseEvidence.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
courseEvidence.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
courseEvidence.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images
courseEvidence.contribution: Teaches mathematical/computational image operations including filters, Hough transform and segmentation. It applies computation to images without claiming the specific fluorescence example or proving VU Fourier theory.

courseEvidence.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
courseEvidence.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
courseEvidence.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
courseEvidence.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design
courseEvidence.contribution: Builds and trains neural networks from scratch and with TensorFlow for tabular, image and text data. The actual profile supports theory and implementation; it does not guarantee a particular gradient-proof syllabus.

courseEvidence.name: Robotics
courseEvidence.description2: Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and manipulation.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies computational problems in robot motion and manipulation, supported by linear algebra, calculus and geometric modelling. Students analyze forward and inverse kinematics, configuration spaces, collision-free motion planning and grasping, with shorter introductions to sensing and control. Practical work programs a robot arm and gripper; research investigates inverse kinematics for an articulated structure. A smaller component examines a chosen legal, ethical, safety or human-robot issue.
courseEvidence.topics: Robot architecture and industrial automation; Rotations, orientations and rigid transformations; Forward and inverse kinematics; Trajectory generation; Configuration spaces and obstacles; Exact, approximate and sampling-based motion planning; Collision detection; Sensing and control; Form and force closure; Caging; Non-prehensile manipulation; Social and ethical aspects of robotics
courseEvidence.methods: Coordinate-frame modelling of articulated structures; Analytic and iterative inverse kinematics; Mathematica computation; Configuration-space modelling; Motion-planning analysis; Collision-detection analysis; Instantaneous-motion and wrench analysis; Robot-arm and gripper programming; Modelling of physical manipulation
courseEvidence.contribution: Studies robotic kinematics and motion planning in configuration space, applying geometric and computational reasoning. This is an application of mathematics; it does not supply the group-theoretic, projective/hyperbolic or topological course sequence.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Programming
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
courseEvidence.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
courseEvidence.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling
courseEvidence.contribution: teaches structured and object-oriented programming in Python together with elements of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving, the Python programming skill that VU teaches in its first-year programming course

courseEvidence.name: Mathematical Methods
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
courseEvidence.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
courseEvidence.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Teaches differentiation, integration, complex numbers and ordinary differential-equation techniques with quantitative projects. This directly supports the calculus foundation; it does not establish rigorous real analysis or a proof-writing sequence.

courseEvidence.name: Linear Algebra
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
courseEvidence.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
courseEvidence.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation
courseEvidence.contribution: Develops vector spaces, linear transformations, matrices, determinants and eigenvalues, including applications to Fourier series, difference equations and Markov chains. This is substantive mathematical theory and computation, not abstract group/ring/field theory.

courseEvidence.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops numerical solutions to mathematical problems that lack convenient analytical solutions, emphasizing when algorithms work and how to validate their output. Students study numerical root finding, interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, ordinary differential equations, and linear and nonlinear systems. Mathematica notebooks apply and compare textbook algorithms with built-in routines, with attention to roundoff, convergence, error, stability and sensitivity.
courseEvidence.topics: Computer arithmetic and roundoff; Algorithm convergence and error; Scalar root finding; Polynomial interpolation and splines; Parametric curves; Numerical differentiation and integration; Initial-value problems; Multistep and adaptive differential-equation methods; Stability and stiff equations; Linear systems and matrix factorization; Nonlinear systems; Numerical-result validation
courseEvidence.methods: Mathematica numerical computation; Bisection, fixed-point, Newton and secant methods; Polynomial and spline interpolation; Numerical differentiation and Richardson extrapolation; Simpson, Romberg and Gaussian quadrature; Adaptive quadrature; Euler and Runge-Kutta methods; Multistep predictor-corrector methods; Gaussian elimination and pivoting; Matrix factorizations; Newton and quasi-Newton methods for systems; Steepest descent; Continuation methods
courseEvidence.contribution: develops numerical root finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and the numerical solution of ordinary differential equations, with explicit attention to accuracy, stability and sensitivity to input

courseEvidence.name: Advanced Calculus
courseEvidence.description2: Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations, including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.
courseEvidence.contribution: Extends calculus to several variables and differential equations using computer algebra. The profile does not establish VU differential forms, general Stokes theorem or proof-based analysis.

courseEvidence.name: Linear Systems
courseEvidence.description2: Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing and modelling.
courseEvidence.profile: Analyzes continuous- and discrete-time signals and linear time-invariant systems through differential or difference equations, impulse responses and frequency-domain representations. Convolution, Fourier series and transforms lead into sampling and reconstruction, filtering, communication systems, Laplace and Z-transforms, and linear feedback. Mathematica laboratories and an applied project connect mathematical properties to signal processing and system behaviour.
courseEvidence.topics: Continuous- and discrete-time signals; System linearity, causality and stability; Impulse and frequency responses; Convolution; Fourier series and transforms; Time-frequency representations; Sampling, reconstruction and aliasing; Digital filtering; Modulation and multiplexing; Laplace and Z-transforms; Regions of convergence and pole-zero representations; Linear feedback and stability
courseEvidence.methods: Convolution sums and integrals; Fourier-series and Fourier-transform analysis; Bode-plot analysis; Sampling and signal reconstruction; Filter analysis; Modulation and demodulation; Laplace and Z-transform analysis; Block-diagram system analysis; Root-locus analysis; Mathematica signal and system computation
courseEvidence.contribution: Studies linear time-invariant systems, convolution, Fourier series and transforms, Laplace and Z-transforms. It supplies genuine transform mathematics, without establishing VU Fourier convergence proofs or nonlinear bifurcation/manifold theory.

courseEvidence.name: Probability & Statistics
courseEvidence.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
courseEvidence.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
courseEvidence.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
courseEvidence.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica
courseEvidence.contribution: provides a foundation in mathematical statistics: probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation

courseEvidence.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
courseEvidence.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.
courseEvidence.topics: Ecology and evolution; Environmental conditions and resources; Climate and life cycles; Ecological niches; Competition and cohabitation; Predation and food webs; Natural selection; Population dynamics; Biodiversity patterns; Ecological succession; Ecosystem energy and matter fluxes; Global cycles; Conservation and human impacts; Ecosystem value
courseEvidence.methods: Ecological modelling in R; Population-dynamics calculations; Ecosystem energy and matter-flux calculations; Ecological research-project design and analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Provides ecological subject knowledge and two weeks of ecological modelling. It is a bounded complementary application setting, not a full mathematical-modelling or dynamical-systems course.

courseEvidence.name: Earth Observation
courseEvidence.description2: Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops geospatial analysis for investigating environmental change and designing responses to Earth-system problems. Hands-on ArcGIS Pro work covers spatial data models, georeferencing, projections, visualization, queries, transformations and surface analysis. Remote-sensing foundations extend into spectral signatures, acquisition systems, preprocessing and image processing. A collaborative case study applies geospatial methods to an environmental research question.
courseEvidence.topics: Spatial concepts and data models; Geospatial databases; Georeferencing and map projections; Spatial visualization; Spatial queries and transformations; Surface analysis; Earth-observation tools; Spectral signatures; Remote-sensing acquisition systems; Image preprocessing and processing; Environmental geospatial applications
courseEvidence.methods: ArcGIS Pro spatial analysis; Spatial-data collection and database management; Georeferencing and coordinate transformation; Geospatial visualization and queries; Surface analysis; Remote-sensing preprocessing; Image processing; Geospatial case-study design
courseEvidence.contribution: Uses GIS to integrate and analyse satellite/drone data on Earth-system change. It is a complementary geospatial application, without claiming the particular fluorescence problem or a mathematical remote-sensing degree.

courseEvidence.name: Earth System Science Tools
courseEvidence.description2: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.
courseEvidence.contribution: Uses Earth-system modelling, proxies and isotope tracers to investigate climate. This is a documented modelling application, not a substitute for abstract dynamical-systems or PDE theory.

courseEvidence.name: Sustainability Essentials I
courseEvidence.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
courseEvidence.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
courseEvidence.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
courseEvidence.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement
courseEvidence.contribution: Introduces planetary boundaries and sustainability as the subject context and formal gateway for Earth-system tools or Earth Observation. It is not advanced mathematical dynamics.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
courseEvidence.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life
courseEvidence.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development
courseEvidence.contribution: examines the nature of knowledge and the theoretical methods philosophers use to support conclusions, including the relation of philosophy to physics and computer science, the philosophical reflection on scientific knowledge that the core's philosophy component addresses

courseEvidence.name: Ethics
courseEvidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
courseEvidence.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
courseEvidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development
courseEvidence.contribution: develops the main ethical theories and applies them to practical questions, the ethics component of the core

courseEvidence.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
courseEvidence.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
courseEvidence.topics: Disease frequency and risk; Incidence and prevalence; Measures of association; Epidemiological study designs; Bias, confounding and causality; Outbreak investigation; Social and environmental health determinants; Health inequalities; Health promotion; Health-needs assessment; Screening; Evidence-informed interventions and implementation
courseEvidence.methods: Epidemiological rate and risk calculation; Descriptive and analytic epidemiology; Study-design and evidence appraisal; Population-health data interpretation; Outbreak analysis; Health-needs assessment; Stakeholder interviewing; Evidence-informed intervention development
courseEvidence.contribution: Develops critical appraisal of evidence about disease, risk and population change. This is a complementary empirical setting; the actual profile does not document mathematical epidemic models or optimisation.

courseEvidence.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
courseEvidence.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
courseEvidence.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
courseEvidence.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting
courseEvidence.contribution: develops multivariate statistical models, including linear and logistic regression, factor analysis, analysis of covariance and non-parametric tests, extending statistical inference to models with many variables

comparability.assessment: Three options share seven mathematical courses and differ by 6, 7 and 8 courses per side across the three pairs. The choices support distinct sequences in modeling, statistical data analysis and optimization with economics. UCR does not sustain a separate pure-mathematics sequence in proof-based analysis, abstract algebra and geometry. Computer science and biomedical applications were considered. The three retained options have stronger coherent mathematics applications; a mathematics-teaching option lacks specialist pedagogy.

repair: Data option: move Computer Vision to term 2, Epidemiology to term 3, Ethics to term 4 and Neural Networks to term 6; replace AI Ethics with Decision-making in AI in term 5. Python precedes decision modelling; mathematical methods and introductory machine learning precede neural networks. All alternatives preserve seven mathematical courses. The modeling option emphasizes numerical and physical applications; the data option emphasizes statistical and computational data analysis; the economics option adds economic reasoning, econometrics and optimization. Examined the strongest available proof evidence in logic, vector spaces, probability and algorithms. It establishes substantive mathematical inquiry but not a sustained sequence of rigorous analysis, abstract algebra or geometry and topology. Operations research and financial mathematics also exceed the economics option. No alternative reproduces the mandatory individual mathematics project.
alignments: Both teach differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential-equation techniques. The VU outline also specifies convergence of series, Taylor series and simple epsilon proofs; those are not established by the UCR profile. This is a qualified subject relationship.

Both treat calculus of several variables. VU explicitly includes differential forms and general Stokes theorem; the UCR profile establishes multivariable calculus/differential equations but not that complete vector-calculus syllabus.

Both develop discrete mathematical reasoning. VU specifies graph theory, combinatorics, flows, generating functions and proofs. The UCR profile supports logic/discrete structures and algorithmic applications, without establishing every listed VU topic.
VU introduces mathematical argument and proof in a dedicated course. UCR develops some of these techniques in Logic & Discrete Mathematics.
VU develops rigorous proofs about calculus and continuity. UCR emphasizes methods and applications.

Complex Analysis studies functions of a complex variable. Advanced Calculus touches complex-valued functions but is a calculus course already matched to Multivariable Calculus; UCR has no complex-analysis course.
VU studies partial differential equations in a dedicated course. UCR’s calculus and numerical courses include ordinary differential equations.

Both study vector spaces, matrices, linear transformations, determinants and eigenvalues. VU also explicitly assesses small proofs, QR/SVD and inner-product methods; the UCR profile does not establish that full assessment/syllabus.
Group Theory is the first abstract-algebra course. UCR has no abstract-algebra course; Advanced Algorithms treats algebraic algorithms computationally and is not claimed as a counterpart.
Rings and Fields continues abstract algebra. UCR has no counterpart.
VU advances its abstract algebra sequence through field extensions and Galois theory.

Elements of Geometry is a geometry course taken as a practical exercise. UCR has no geometry course; Robotics uses geometric reasoning about configuration spaces for motion planning but is not a geometry course, so no counterpart is claimed.
Topology studies topological spaces and continuity abstractly. UCR has no counterpart.
Differential Topology is an advanced course on smooth manifolds. UCR has no counterpart.
Dynamical systems, Fourier analysis & modelling of real systems

Both study Fourier series and Fourier transforms. UCR approaches them through linear time-invariant systems and convolution, adding Laplace/Z-transforms; VU develops convergence, summability, Plancherel theory, proofs and PDE applications. This is partial mathematical correspondence.

Dynamical Systems is the core course on the mathematical theory of systems evolving in time. Linear Systems treats only linear time-invariant systems and is already matched to Fourier Analysis, and no other UCR course develops dynamical-systems theory, so no counterpart is claimed.

Mathematical Modelling of Dynamical Systems translates real systems, such as predator-prey populations, into dynamical models. Ecosystems Uncovered spends two weeks on ecological modelling and Earth System Science Tools teaches Earth-system modelling, but both are science courses in which modelling is one component rather than the mathematical subject itself, so neither is claimed as a counterpart.

Both teach mathematical probability and discrete/continuous distributions. VU details joint/conditional distributions and the central limit theorem; UCR additionally includes estimation and simulation, without documentation of every VU theoretical topic.

VU develops frequentist and Bayesian estimators, tests, confidence sets and their mathematical comparison. UCR’s probability course is already paired to Probability Theory; applied Research Methods and Statistics does not establish this mathematical-statistics course. No separate counterpart is claimed.

Mathematical Modelling of Stochastic Systems models random processes evolving in time. Decision-making in AI concerns planning under uncertainty rather than stochastic-process modelling, and Linear Algebra treats Markov chains only as an application, so no counterpart is claimed.
Both teach programming in Python from scratch. UCR's course is a full course that also covers object-oriented programming and elements of discrete mathematics; VU's is a 3-EC introduction.

Both teach numerical root finding, interpolation, numerical integration and ODE solution with accuracy/reliability. VU additionally specifies Matlab, eigenvalue/least-squares problems, FFT and PDE applications; these are not all established in the UCR profile.

Introduction to Mathematical Modelling, LaTeX and Mathematica teaches mathematical software and typesetting for modelling work. UCR mathematics courses use computer algebra software within their content, but no UCR course is dedicated to mathematical software and typesetting.

Both address ethics as part of the programme. Philosophy and Ethics is a 3-EC course for science students; UCR's Ethics is a full course in moral theory and practical ethics and shares its ethical component, not any philosophy-of-science content.
History of Science is a 3-EC course on the historical development of science. No UCR course in these alternatives treats the history of science, so no counterpart is claimed.
Personal development, open profiling space & research
VU reserves 30 EC for approved open study.
VU requires a 12 EC individual mathematics project and thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.

candidates.label: Proof-based pure mathematics
candidates.assessment: UCR offers genuine calculus, vector-space theory, probability and Fourier/algorithmic methods, but no documented sustained proof-writing, rigorous real/complex analysis, abstract algebra, geometry/topology or nonlinear theoretical sequence. Applied methods cannot own these pure-mathematics interests. This limitation is explicit in every retained alternative.
